text: This document teaches core banking and money management concepts for learners who want to use banks and credit unions safely and effectively. It explains why people use banks, how to open and maintain an account, how checking and savings accounts work, and what fees, interest, and balances mean. It also describes common banking services such as direct deposit, ATMs, money orders, online banking, debit cards, money transfers, loans, and stored value cards. The guide includes practical advice on choosing a bank, avoiding unnecessary fees, comparing accounts, protecting personal information, and asking questions before signing up for financial products.

A bank is a business that offers a safe place to keep money and uses deposits to make loans. In this curriculum, the term bank also includes credit unions and thrifts. Banks offer many financial services and can help a person build a positive relationship with a financial institution.

Safety: Money is safer from theft, loss, and fire.
Convenience: Money can be accessed quickly and easily, and direct deposit can make funds available sooner than depositing a check.
Cost: Using a bank is probably cheaper than using other businesses to cash checks.
Security: FDIC-insured banks protect deposits up to the maximum amount allowed by law, and most credit unions are insured by NCUA under the same deposit insurance rules.
Financial future: A relationship with a bank can help establish a record of paying bills, help with saving money, and is necessary for getting a loan.

Bank: A financial institution run under federal and state laws and regulations that makes loans, pays checks, accepts deposits, and provides other financial services.
Credit union: A non-profit financial institution owned by people who have something in common; membership is required to keep money there.
Thrift: A savings bank or savings and loan association similar to a bank, created to promote home ownership, with most assets in housing-related loans.

section_title: How to open and maintain a bank account
text: Opening and maintaining a bank account involves four basic tasks: open the account and complete account verification, make deposits and withdrawals, record interest and fees, and keep track of the account balance. These steps help a person use an account responsibly and avoid unnecessary charges.

To open a bank account, a person usually goes through account verification. A bank may review checking account history through companies such as TeleCheck or ChexSystems and may also run a full credit report. The bank will need photo identification, such as a driver’s license, and a Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number to verify identity. Some banks may accept other photo identification, such as a matrícula consular card, Green Card, or passport. If a person cannot open an account, the guide recommends asking about second chance checking programs and checking with local financial institutions or reputable credit counseling agencies for available programs.

Choose a bank that offers the services needed.
Check whether the bank is close to home.
Check whether the bank has reasonable hours.
Check whether the bank has ATMs near where the person lives, works, or shops.
For a credit union, check whether the person is eligible for membership.
Ask whether any employees speak the person’s language.
Ask what fees will be charged.
Confirm that the bank is insured.

A deposit is money added to an account, usually using a deposit slip that tells the bank how much money is being added. Depending on whether the deposit is cash, a payroll check, or another type of check, funds may not be available immediately, so the guide says to ask the bank when deposited money can be used. A withdrawal is money taken out of an account by writing a check, using a withdrawal slip, or using an ATM. A balance is the amount of money in the account, and it should be tracked carefully to avoid taking out more than is available.

Financial institutions charge fees for different services, including monthly maintenance fees and penalty fees for misusing an account. If a person writes a check or makes a transaction for more money than is available, the account is overdrawn and fees may be charged. Some institutions offer courtesy overdraft protection or bounce protection, but these services still charge overdraft or bounce protection fees and do not guarantee that all overdrawn transactions will be covered. Interest is a percentage of the account balance paid by the bank for keeping money there, although not all accounts pay interest.

The guide says it is usually much cheaper to use a deposit account at a bank than a check-cashing service. In its example, cashing four checks a month at $5 each costs $240 a year, and buying five money orders a month at $1 each adds $60, for a total yearly cost of $300. By comparison, a checking account with a $5 monthly fee plus $18 for a box of checks costs $78 a year, which is a savings of $222.

A checking account lets a person write checks to pay bills or buy goods, and the financial institution provides a monthly bank statement showing deposits and withdrawals. A savings account always earns interest, generally does not allow check writing, and may require only a few dollars to open, although a monthly fee may be charged if the balance falls below a required amount. Banks may also require a minimum balance to open an account, earn interest, or avoid fees, so comparing account rules is important.

Ask how much money is needed to open the account.
Ask how much money must stay in the account to avoid fees.
Ask what the fees are for bounced checks.
Ask how many checks can be written before extra fees are charged.
Ask how many withdrawals can be made each month.
Ask whether the account pays interest.
Ask whether an ATM card or debit card comes with the account.
Ask whether there are fees for using the ATM or debit card at the same bank or at another bank.
Ask whether there are any other fees.

Many banks also offer non-deposit products such as stocks, bonds, and mutual funds. These products are not insured by the FDIC and may lose value. The guide advises not buying any product or service that is not understood.

Direct deposit is a method used by an employer or government agency to send a paycheck or benefit payment electronically into an account. The amount is immediately available, and some banks may not charge monthly fees if direct deposit is used. The guide also notes that electronically filing a federal tax return and using direct deposit can make a refund available in 8 to 15 days, while receiving a mailed check can take 6 weeks, and some same-day refund offers come with significant charges.

An ATM is a kiosk or terminal where a person can deposit, withdraw, or transfer money 24 hours a day. There may be fees for ATM use, especially when using another bank’s ATM, and some deposits may only be possible at the account holder’s own bank ATM. The guide also notes that some banks offer dual ATM cards for family members outside the United States, which may be cheaper than sending a wire transfer.

Telephone banking allows a person to check balances by phone, transfer money between accounts, review recent deposits or withdrawals, stop payment on a check, get branch information, and report a lost, stolen, or damaged card. Online banking allows many of the same tasks on a computer, including checking balances, transferring funds, paying bills, submitting a loan application, and sending secure electronic messages to the bank.

section_title: Money orders, cashier’s checks, and certified checks
text: A money order is used like a check to pay a bill or make a purchase when cash is not accepted, and many businesses sell money orders for a fee, so the guide recommends shopping around for the best price. A cashier’s check is issued by a financial institution after the person provides the amount of the check plus a service charge, usually $2 to $5, and it is guaranteed not to bounce. A certified check is a personal check marked certified by the bank for a fee, usually $2 to $5, with the money held in the account until the check is processed, and it is also guaranteed not to bounce.

A money transfer is an electronic transfer of money from one bank to another. A remittance is a money transfer sent to a bank or person in another country, and the guide says banks may send money more cheaply than companies such as Western Union or MoneyGram. Before sending a remittance, the guide recommends asking about the total cost including all fees, the total amount the recipient will receive in the destination country, how soon the money will arrive, the background and reputation of the company, whether licensing is required and in place, and whether a receipt or document with all remittance information will be provided.

A debit card, sometimes called a check card, is tied to a checking account and removes money from the account immediately when used for purchases. Unlike credit cards, debit cards are described as “buy now, pay now” and do not charge interest, but a person may overdraw the account if debit card transactions are not recorded carefully. If someone uses a debit card without permission, the guide says to inform the bank immediately; if the bank cannot resolve the matter within 10 business days after being told, it will put the money back into the account less $50. A debit card can also function as an ATM card and often requires a PIN, so the guide advises making sure no one can see the PIN when it is entered.

A stored value card is a card that can be loaded with money for future purchases. Examples include telephone cards with prepaid minutes, international gift cards, and payroll cards. The guide says stored value cards may reduce check-cashing fees, provide 24-hour access to funds, make money transfers more available to families, reduce the need to carry cash, and work like a pseudo bank account, but they may also charge many fees, may not be FDIC-insured, and may not protect against loss or theft. Before getting one, the guide recommends asking whether the money is FDIC-insured, what fees will be charged, and what rights apply if the card is lost or stolen.
A loan is money borrowed from a bank with a written promise to repay it later. Banks charge fees and interest for loans, which is the cost of borrowing money.

Privacy notices explain how a financial company handles, shares, and protects personal financial information. A person receives an initial privacy notice when opening an account and another each year, and federal privacy laws give the right to opt out of some information sharing. To limit promotions or data sharing, the guide says to review the privacy notice for sharing practices and follow the opt-out instructions if they apply. It also says a person can opt out of prescreened credit or insurance offers by calling 1-888-5-OPTOUT or visiting optoutprescreen.com, but some information sharing is still allowed by law and information shared before opting out cannot be retrieved.

Customer service representative: Helps open accounts, explains services, answers general questions, refers customers to the right person, and provides written information about bank products.
Teller: Accepts deposits, cashes checks, answers questions, and refers customers for other bank services.
Loan officer: Takes loan applications, answers questions, provides written information about loan products, and helps complete loan applications.
Branch manager: Supervises branch operations and helps solve problems other bank employees cannot solve.

Ask the bank what identification is needed before trying to open an account.
Ask whether second chance checking programs are available if an account application is denied.
Ask when deposited funds will be available for use.
Keep track of balances so withdrawals and debit purchases do not overdraw the account.
Compare banks and accounts by fees, minimum balances, ATM access, services, and insurance status.
Do not buy a financial product or service that is not understood.
Shop around for the best price on money orders.
Ask detailed questions before sending a remittance, including fees, exchange rate effects, delivery timing, licensing, and receipt documentation.
Report unauthorized debit card use immediately.
Review privacy notices and use opt-out options when desired.
Ask questions until the information is clear, do not sign anything that is not understood, and ask for written information to review at home.

bank: A business that offers a safe place to keep money and uses deposits to make loans.
financial institution: A bank, credit union, or thrift that provides financial services.
account verification: The process a bank uses to confirm identity and assess whether a person can open an account.
deposit: Money added to an account.
withdrawal: Money taken out of an account.
balance: The amount of money in a bank account.
overdraft: Taking out or spending more money than is available in the account.
interest: A percentage of the account balance paid by the bank for keeping money there.
checking account: A deposit account that lets a person write checks and make payments.
savings account: A deposit account that earns interest and usually does not allow check writing.
minimum balance: The amount that may be required to open an account, earn interest, or avoid fees.
direct deposit: Electronic deposit of a paycheck or benefit payment into an account.
money transfer: Electronic movement of money from one bank to another.
remittance: A money transfer sent to a bank or person in another country.
debit card: A card tied to a checking account that removes money immediately when used.
stored value card: A card loaded with money for future purchases.
privacy notice: A notice explaining how a financial company collects, shares, and protects personal financial information.
opt out: The right to stop some sharing of personal financial information.

Keep money in an insured bank or credit union for safety, convenience, cost savings, and long-term financial benefits.
Use bank and account checklists to compare services, locations, hours, fees, insurance, ATM access, and minimum balance rules.
Bring acceptable identification and tax identification information when opening an account, and ask what documents are required.
Ask about second chance checking if a regular account cannot be opened.
Track every deposit, withdrawal, fee, and interest payment to maintain an accurate balance.
Avoid overdrawing an account because bounced checks and overdrawn transactions can trigger fees.
Compare the cost of bank accounts with check-cashing services before deciding where to manage money.
Ask about fees before using ATMs, money orders, stored value cards, and other services.
Shop around for the best price on money orders and ask about all remittance fees and exchange-rate effects before sending money internationally.
Report unauthorized debit card use immediately and protect the PIN from being seen by others.
Review privacy notices and follow opt-out instructions if limiting information sharing is important.
Ask questions until terms are clear, ask for written information, and do not sign anything that is not understood.

This worksheet helps users identify common spending challenges and choose practical actions to better manage spending. It explains that improving financial well-being includes having more control over day-to-day and month-to-month finances, building a cushion for financial shocks, getting on track to meet financial goals, and having more freedom to make choices that allow enjoyment of life. The document guides users through identifying spending problems, creating a budget, setting spending limits, and monitoring progress. It ends with a simple personal action plan where users list specific steps they will take to manage spending.

This worksheet is designed to help users recognize common spending challenges and come up with ways to take action to manage spending. It connects spending management to financial well-being and presents a short process for identifying problems, choosing budgeting actions, and creating a personal plan.

Improving financial well-being means having more control over day-to-day and month-to-month finances, having a greater cushion to absorb a financial shock, getting on track to meet financial goals, and having more financial freedom to make choices that allow enjoyment of life.

Users are instructed to review a list of common spending challenges and check the ones that apply to them. If one or more challenges apply, the worksheet directs users to try the spending-management tips that follow.

Not tracking or budgeting income and spending because it feels like a hassle.
Having tried to use a budget, but finding income and spending tracking too complicated or too time-consuming.
Struggling to pay bills and expenses because income is inadequate or irregular.
Overspending and assuming spending can be reduced later, but finding that hard to do.
Not thinking about money spent when using a debit card or credit card for purchases.
Treating oneself or others occasionally even when it is not affordable.
Avoiding thinking about the financial situation because it feels discouraging.

The worksheet provides four ways to address spending challenges: track spending, create a budget, decide how much to spend, and keep track of progress. These steps are meant to help users manage spending more consistently and align spending with financial goals.

Start by getting a handle on where money goes. Track spending for a week or a month to see how much is being spent in different categories. The worksheet does not provide fixed category names, so users should organize spending into the categories that best reflect their household spending patterns.

Create a household budget. Decide how much money can be set aside or saved for special occasions so life can be enjoyed without overspending. This step is presented as the foundation for setting later spending limits and comparing actual spending against planned spending.

section_title: Decide how much to spend on small purchases
text: Set a weekly spending limit based on the budget for small purchases that can add up and keep a person from achieving aspirations. The worksheet suggests setting aside cash for these purchases at the beginning of the week and not spending more than that amount. It also instructs users to check balances before shopping and set a spending limit based on the budget.

Compare actual spending to the budget monthly or more frequently. If spending is regularly out of line with the budget, make adjustments to the budget. The worksheet also recommends checking balances regularly on accounts, credit cards, and prepaid cards, and signing up for balance alert text message services from a financial institution. It notes that some balance-checking services may incur fees and users should check with their financial service provider.

section_title: Budget categories to track in this worksheet
text:
Income and spending: Track total money coming in and total money going out.
Spending categories: Track spending by category over a week or a month to see where money goes. The worksheet instructs users to use different categories but does not specify exact category labels.
Bills and expenses: Monitor required payments and recurring expenses, especially if income is inadequate or irregular.
Small purchases: Set a weekly spending limit for smaller purchases that can accumulate over time.
Special occasion savings: Decide how much to set aside or save for special occasions.
Account balances: Check balances on bank accounts, credit cards, and prepaid cards before spending and on a regular basis.

Check which spending challenges apply.
Track spending for a week or a month in spending categories.
Create a household budget.
Decide how much money to save for special occasions.
Set a weekly spending limit for small purchases.
Consider setting aside cash for small purchases at the start of the week and do not spend more than that amount.
Check balances before shopping and use the budget to set a spending limit.
Compare actual spending to the budget monthly or more often, and adjust the budget if needed.
Check account, credit card, and prepaid card balances regularly.
Sign up for balance alerts from a financial institution if available.

This worksheet ends with a personal planning section titled “Create a personal plan for managing spending.” It asks the user to pick one or more of the suggested solutions or come up with their own ideas. The form contains four action fields labeled as steps the user will take to manage spending.

Step 1 action the user will take to manage spending.
Step 2 action the user will take to manage spending.
Step 3 action the user will take to manage spending.
Step 4 action the user will take to manage spending.

financial well-being: Having more control over finances, a greater cushion for shocks, progress toward financial goals, and more freedom to make life choices.
spending challenges: Common problems that make it harder to stay on budget or manage money effectively.
household budget: A budget a user creates to plan spending and saving.
spending limit: A set amount a user decides not to exceed, such as a weekly limit for small purchases.
actual spending: The amount a user really spends, which should be compared with the budget.
balance alerts: Text message services from a financial institution that notify a user about account balances.

Track spending for a week or a month to see how much is being spent in different categories.
Create a household budget.
Decide how much money to set aside or save for special occasions.
Set a weekly spending limit for small purchases that can add up over time.
Consider setting aside cash for small purchases at the beginning of the week and do not spend more than that amount.
Check balances before shopping and set a spending limit based on the budget.
Compare actual spending to the budget monthly or more frequently and adjust the budget if it is regularly out of line.
Check balances regularly on accounts, credit cards, and prepaid cards.
Sign up for balance alert text message services from a financial institution.

This guide teaches how budgets help people plan spending and saving so they can cover needs, pay for wants, and save money regularly. It explains that a budget should be based on net income, which is the amount of money brought home after taxes and other deductions. The document introduces the 50-30-20 budgeting rule as one example of how to divide money among needs, wants, and savings. It also teaches key budgeting vocabulary and uses a station activity with budget cards to help learners practice making spending choices within category limits. The guide emphasizes that the 50-30-20 rule is only one possible rule and that people should use guidelines that fit their own financial situation.

Knowing how to make a budget is an important step in reaching financial goals. A budget is a plan for how to spend and save money. It helps a person decide how much to spend on necessities, how much to put aside for savings, and how much to use for wants. A budget should be made using net income, which is the amount of money brought home in a paycheck after taxes and other deductions are taken out. A budget should also be reviewed when finances change, such as after getting a new job, moving, or taking out a loan.

Following a budget helps make sure there is money for things a person needs and wants while still saving regularly. The guide explains that even middle school students can make a budget, such as when managing allowance money or earnings from jobs like babysitting or mowing lawns. Budgeting can help with paying for needed items, spending on enjoyable activities, and saving for future goals such as college or other planned purchases.

One budgeting rule presented in the guide is to use 50 percent of income for needs, 30 percent for wants, and 20 percent for savings for financial goals. The guide notes that this is only one rule to live by and that not everyone can follow it. People should decide on a personal rule that works for their own financial situation and use simple spending guidelines that help them reach savings goals.

Needs: Rent or mortgage payments, groceries, utilities, transportation, food, medical expenses, car insurance.
Wants: Dining out, vacations, entertainment, a new video game, specialty coffee, cell phone.
Savings: Emergency savings, paying down debt, saving for education, saving for retirement, saving for a large purchase.

A monthly budget is a spending plan that outlines how a person will save or spend the money earned that month. The guide organizes budgets into three categories: needs, wants, and savings. It explains that people often create budget rules to help manage money and make decisions about spending within those categories.

Budget: A plan that outlines what money a person expects to earn or receive and how that money will be saved or spent for a given period of time; also called a spending plan.
Long-term goals: Goals that can take more than five years to achieve.
Short-term goals: Goals that can take a short time, or up to five years, to reach.
Needs: Basic things people must have to survive, resources they may need to do their jobs, and resources to help build and protect their money and property so they can meet future needs.
Wants: Upgrades and other things that would be nice to have but are not necessary for living, income, or protecting what a person has.
Savings: Money set aside in a secure place, such as a bank account, for future emergencies or specific purchases.

The guide uses an interactive activity in which students work with a budget of 100 points. Their goal is to make spending choices that follow the 50-30-20 rule by spending up to 50 points on needs, 30 points on wants, and 20 points on savings. Students visit needs, wants, and savings stations, choose options from budget cards, record point values, and then answer reflection questions. For this activity, emergency savings is placed in the savings category even though it is often considered a need.

section_title: Needs expense categories in the activity
text:
Housing expenses: housing
Food expenses: food
Transportation expenses: transportation
Utility expenses: electric, water, gas
Clothing expenses: clothing

section_title: Wants expense categories in the activity
text:
Communication expenses: cell phone
Internet expenses: internet
Entertainment expenses: entertainment
Dining expenses: eating out at restaurants
Shopping expenses: shopping

Long-term savings: such as saving for college.
Short-term savings: such as saving for new sneakers.
Emergency savings: such as saving for unexpected events.

Students begin with an income of 100 points per month, so the monthly point breakdown is needs = 50 points, wants = 30 points, and savings = 20 points. The answer guide indicates these choices for the budget cards: Needs: Card 1 Option B, Card 2 Option A, Card 3 Option B, Card 4 Option B. Wants: Card 1 Option A, Card 2 Option B, Card 3 Option A, Card 4 Option A. Savings: Card 1 Option A, Card 2 Option B, Card 3 Option B, Card 4 Option A.

The guide asks learners to compare the options they chose with the options they did not choose and think about what those choices might look like in real life. It suggests that living within a budget may require compromises such as living in a smaller or more modest house, having a basic cell phone plan, or planning some meatless meals to save money. It also asks how a budget rule like 50-30-20 might help manage money when living independently, including making sure there is money for needs and wants while still saving regularly.

The guide suggests using additional Consumer Financial Protection Bureau activities related to saving and spending. Examples named in the guide are “Creating a monthly household budget” and “Brainstorming household budgets.”

budget: A plan that outlines expected income and how money will be saved or spent for a given period of time; also called a spending plan.
monthly budget: A spending plan that outlines how money earned in a month will be saved or spent.
net income: The amount of money brought home in a paycheck after taxes and other deductions are taken out.
needs: Basic things required for survival, work, and protection of money and property for future needs.
wants: Upgrades and other things that are nice to have but are not necessary for living, income, or protection.
savings: Money set aside in a secure place for emergencies or specific future purchases.
long-term goals: Goals that can take more than five years to achieve.
short-term goals: Goals that can take a short time, or up to five years, to reach.
50-30-20 rule: A budgeting rule that uses 50 percent of income for needs, 30 percent for wants, and 20 percent for savings.

Create a budget using net income rather than gross income.
Organize spending into three categories: needs, wants, and savings.
Use the 50-30-20 rule as one possible budgeting guideline: 50 percent for needs, 30 percent for wants, and 20 percent for savings.
Review a budget when financial circumstances change, such as after a new job, a move, or taking out a loan.
Set personal spending guidelines that fit the individual financial situation and support savings goals.
Compare spending choices within each category to decide which options best fit the budget rule.

This worksheet helps a user see how much money they spend in the current month and use that information to plan the next month’s budget. It organizes income and expenses into clear categories so a user can total monthly income, total monthly expenses, and compare the two. The worksheet also explains that expenses that do not occur every month should be placed in the “Other expenses this month” category. It ends with simple guidance for interpreting the result: if income is greater than expenses, money is left to save or spend, and if expenses are greater than income, the budget should be reviewed to find expenses to cut.

Use this worksheet to see how much money is spent this month. Then use this month’s information to help plan next month’s budget. Some bills are monthly and some come less often, so any expense that does not occur every month should be entered under “Other expenses this month.”

Enter the month and year for the budget period.
Record income for the month.
Record each expense under the matching category.
Add all income amounts to calculate total monthly income.
Add all expense amounts to calculate total monthly expenses.
Compare total monthly income with total monthly expenses.
If an expense does not occur every month, include it in “Other expenses this month.”

Paychecks: Salary after taxes, benefits, and check cashing fees.
Other income: Income after taxes, for example child support.
Total monthly income: The total of all income recorded for the month.

Rent or mortgage.
Renter's insurance or homeowner's insurance.
Utilities, such as electricity and gas.
Internet, cable, and phones.
Other housing expenses, such as property taxes.

Groceries and household supplies.
Meals out.
Other food expenses.

Public transportation and taxis.
Gas for car.
Parking and tolls.
Car maintenance, such as oil changes.
Car insurance.
Car loan.
Other transportation expenses.

Medicine.
Health insurance.
Other health expenses, such as doctors' appointments and eyeglasses.

Child care.
Child support.
Money given or sent to family.
Clothing and shoes.
Laundry.
Donations.
Entertainment, such as movies and amusement parks.
Other personal or family expenses, such as beauty care.

Fees for cashier's checks and money transfers.
Prepaid cards and phone cards.
Bank or credit card fees.
Other fees.
School costs, such as supplies, tuition, and student loans.
Other payments, such as credit cards and savings.

The worksheet includes a line for “Other expenses this month” for expenses that are irregular or do not occur every month. It also includes a line for total monthly expenses so the user can compare all spending against total monthly income.
Maybe income is more than expenses, which means money is left to save or spend. Maybe expenses are more than income, which means the budget should be reviewed to find expenses to cut.

total monthly income: The total amount of income recorded for the month.
total monthly expenses: The total amount of all expenses recorded for the month.
other expenses this month: A category for expenses that do not occur every month.
housing expenses: Costs related to housing, utilities, insurance, communications, and other housing-related items.
food expenses: Costs related to groceries, meals out, and other food spending.
transportation expenses: Costs related to travel, vehicle use, maintenance, insurance, and loans.
health expenses: Costs related to medicine, health insurance, and other healthcare needs.
personal and family expenses: Costs related to dependents, family support, clothing, laundry, donations, entertainment, and personal care.
finance fees: Costs related to money transfers, prepaid products, and bank or credit card fees.

Use the worksheet to calculate how much money is spent this month.
Use this month’s spending information to plan next month’s budget.
Put any non-monthly expense in the “Other expenses this month” category.
Record salary after taxes, benefits, and check cashing fees under paychecks.
Record other income after taxes under other income.
Add income entries to get total monthly income.
Add expense entries to get total monthly expenses.
Compare income and expenses to see whether money is left to save or spend or whether expenses need to be cut.
